fable-5.1.text:
So, the value function... I think it's useful, and the way to think about it is, when you do reinforcement learning the naive way, you have to wait until the end of the whole thing to find out whether you did well. You take a long sequence of actions, and only at the very end you get a signal, good or bad. The value function is what lets you shortcut that. It's the thing that tells you, in the middle of what you're doing, "this is going well" or "this is going badly," without having to see the final outcome.

A simple example is chess. Suppose you play a game and you lose a piece. You don't need to wait until you've been checkmated forty moves later to know that something went wrong. You know right away, this was a mistake, and the credit assignment can happen right there. Or if you're trying to prove a theorem and you spend a lot of time on some approach and it doesn't pan out, you can tell quite early that the approach is not working. You don't have to run it all the way through. That's the value function doing its job.

Now, here's something that I find interesting. My understanding is that in a lot of the current RL that people do with language models, the value function is not actually being used that much. People have tried. I think the DeepSeek R1 paper explicitly says they didn't use one, and I think the reason has to do with the trajectories being very long and very branching, so it's actually hard to learn a good value function. But that's a limitation of the current methods, not a statement about whether value functions are useful in principle. In principle they should be very useful.

And I'd say one more thing, which is that I think the human analog of a value function is emotions. Emotions are the way evolution gave us a value function. It's hardcoded, it's not very precise, but it tells you, "this situation is good, this situation is bad," long before you see any final outcome. And it's robust, in a way that is interesting. So I think the value function is one of those things where the idea is clearly right, and it's a question of how well it ends up being used.

r001.rationale: It says the value function can signal whether things are going well or badly mid-task, without waiting for the final outcome.

r002.rationale: It says a theorem-proving approach can be recognized as unproductive early, but does not explain that this recognition supplies a negative learning signal for the earlier decision to pursue it.

opus-5.5.text:
So, the way reinforcement learning is often done today, at least in the simplest form, is that you let the model take a long sequence of actions, maybe it's trying to solve some problem, and only at the very end do you score the outcome. Then you use that score to provide a training signal for every action along the way. The obvious consequence is that you learn nothing until you've finished the whole thing. If the task is long, and you only find out at the end whether you did well, that's slow and inefficient.

The value function lets you short-circuit that. It lets you say, partway through, "I'm doing well" or "I'm doing badly," without waiting for the final result. Chess is a nice example. If you lose a piece, you know immediately that you messed up. You don't need to play the whole game to find out. You can trace the bad outcome back to the specific decision that caused it. Or in math or programming: you go down some direction, and after a thousand steps of thinking you conclude it isn't promising. A good value function would let you take that signal and apply it back at the moment you chose that direction, so next time you don't go down it.

I think this is very important, and I'd go further. I think humans have something like a value function, and it's a big part of why we learn so efficiently. One thing I find interesting is the role of emotions. There are cases of people who, through some kind of brain damage, lose much of their emotional processing. They can still reason, still talk, still solve puzzles, yet they become extremely bad at making decisions. Something as simple as choosing which socks to wear can take hours. To me that suggests that emotions are, in a sense, a kind of value function, hardcoded by evolution. They're relatively simple, yet they're remarkably robust and useful across an enormous range of situations, including ones very different from the environment they evolved in.

So I believe that value functions, or whatever their right generalization turns out to be, will matter a great deal. Right now people do somewhat use them, but not in the deep way I think is possible. Learning them well is hard, because the judgment "this is going well" is itself a very difficult prediction to make. But I'm fairly confident that whatever the right approach is, it will make use of something like this, and it will make learning far more efficient than what we do today.

r001.rationale: It says a value function can assess progress partway through, signaling whether things are going well or badly before the final result.

r002.rationale: It explains that recognizing a line of thought as unpromising lets the agent apply that negative signal to the earlier choice to pursue it.

fable-5.text:
The way to think about the value function is that it lets you learn from something before it's finished. In the most basic formulation of reinforcement learning, you do a whole long trajectory — maybe thousands of actions — and at the very end you get a score, and that score is what teaches you. The value function says: actually, you don't need to wait until the end. If somewhere in the middle you can already tell how things are going, you can learn from that right away.

A concrete example: suppose you're playing chess, and you make some blunder and lose your queen for nothing. You don't need to play out the next forty moves and lose the game to know that something went wrong. You know it right there, the moment it happened. So the learning signal can propagate to the decision that actually caused the problem, immediately, rather than being diluted across the whole trajectory. Or if you're writing code and you pursue some approach and it turns out to be a dead end — the moment you realize it's a dead end, that realization is a training signal. You don't need to finish the program and run the tests to learn that the branch point, way back, was the mistake.

Now, one thing I'd say is that the value function is, in some sense, an efficiency thing. Anything you can learn with a value function, you could in principle learn without one — you just wait until the end, and you'd need many more trajectories, and the credit assignment would be much noisier. So it doesn't let you do something fundamentally impossible otherwise. But the efficiency difference can be very large, especially as the horizons get long. If the task takes many hours and the mistakes happen in the first few minutes, learning only from the final outcome is extremely wasteful.

And there's something suggestive here about people. You could speculate that emotions are something like a value function. You do something, and you immediately feel that it was bad — you feel regret, or you feel that things are going well — long before the actual consequences arrive. It's your brain giving you an intermediate evaluation of the state you're in. It's not a perfect analogy, and I'd hold it loosely, but I think it points at why this kind of intermediate evaluation is so useful: it's how you learn from experience at the timescale of the decisions themselves, rather than at the timescale of the outcomes.

r001.rationale: It says the value function lets an agent learn before the task is finished by providing an intermediate signal.

r002.rationale: It explains that realizing a code approach is a dead end provides a training signal for the earlier branch-point decision to pursue it.

opus-5.text:
Value functions are interesting. I think they are underutilized right now — not totally unused, but underutilized relative to how useful they should be.

Let me explain what a value function does, conceptually. Right now, the dominant way of doing RL is: you have a task, the model does a very long rollout, maybe it thinks for a long time, and at the end you find out whether it succeeded or not, and then you take that single signal and you apply it to the whole trajectory. That's wasteful in an obvious way. You had to do all that work to get one bit of information.

The value function says: you shouldn't have to wait until the end. Sometimes you can tell much earlier. In chess, if you blunder your queen for nothing, you don't need to play out the remaining forty moves to learn that something went wrong. You know right there. And more to the point, you can learn from that moment directly, which means your learning is much more efficient — you're getting signal continuously rather than once per episode.

There's a human analogy, which is that when you're working on something and your approach starts to feel like it isn't going anywhere, you get this feeling of discouragement, and you reconsider. That feeling is a value function. It's doing exactly this job, and it's doing it well before the outcome is known.

But here's the catch, and this is maybe why it hasn't produced dramatic gains yet. The value function has to actually understand the domain to be right. In chess losing the queen is usually bad — except when it's a brilliant sacrifice, and then it's the best move on the board. So a value function that's too shallow will confidently mispredict exactly in the interesting cases. In math or research, judging mid-proof whether an approach is a dead end requires real insight, not pattern matching.

So I do think value functions will matter. But the reason they haven't yet is the same reason everything else is hard — it comes back to generalization.

r001.rationale: The response says a value function can provide feedback before the task ends, rather than waiting for the final outcome, and describes receiving signal continuously.

r002.rationale: It describes noticing an approach is going nowhere and reconsidering, but does not clearly say that this recognition supplies a negative learning signal for the earlier decision to pursue that direction.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think value functions are going to be used much more than they are today. Here is the intuition. In the simple way of doing reinforcement learning, you give the model a problem, it thinks or acts for a very long time, maybe thousands or tens of thousands of steps, and only at the end do you get a score. Then you take that one number and push it back across the entire trajectory. That works, but it's very wasteful. If the model went down a bad path early on, you don't find out until the very end, and all the compute spent after the mistake is spent on something you already could have known was doomed.

A value function is meant to short-circuit that. It's an estimate, partway through, of how well things are going to turn out. Think about chess. If you lose a piece, you know right away that you probably made a mistake, and you don't need to play the game out to learn from it. Or take someone working on a hard programming problem who explores a direction for a while and then realizes it's a dead end. The useful learning signal is already there at that moment. You'd like to say "this was the wrong direction" right then, and let that feed back to the point where the direction was chosen.

So in principle it makes learning much more efficient, because you get a training signal at intermediate steps instead of waiting for the end. It also helps when the tasks are long and the reward is sparse, which is exactly where things are heading.

The caveat is that it's hard. A value function has to be learned, and it has to be good. If it's noisy or biased, you end up optimizing against a bad critic. That's part of why it hasn't been the main thing people reach for in this latest wave of training. But I don't think it's a fundamental obstacle. I'd expect that as we do more long-horizon reinforcement learning, getting a good estimate of "how am I doing right now?" will matter a lot, and it's something we should be taking more seriously.

r001.rationale: It says a value function estimates outcomes partway through and provides training signals at intermediate steps, before the task ends.

r002.rationale: It describes realizing a programming direction is a dead end and using that signal to give feedback to the earlier choice to pursue it.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it's more useful than people give it credit for. The basic problem with the standard setup is that you play out an entire trajectory, see only whether it ended well or badly, and then push that one number back through every action you took. That's a very noisy signal, and you need a huge number of samples to pull out what actually mattered.

A value function lets you judge a situation before the episode ends. At each step you can ask how promising things look from here, and that gives you feedback along the way instead of only at the end. People learn this way. If you blunder in the middle of a chess game, you usually feel it within a move or two. You don't need to wait until you lose.

The catch is that the value function is itself learned, so it can be wrong. If it's badly miscalibrated, you introduce bias, and the agent can learn to chase the estimator's mistakes instead of the real objective. So the benefit depends a lot on how good the estimates are. When they're good, the gain in sample efficiency can be dramatic. When they're poor, you're mostly trading one problem for another.

r001.rationale: It says a value function can judge a situation before the episode ends, providing feedback along the way.

r002.rationale: The chess blunder analogy suggests noticing a mistake before the game ends, but the response does not explain that recognizing a reasoning direction as unpromising gives a negative learning signal for the earlier decision to pursue it.

astra-6.text:
I think a value function is useful because it lets you learn something about the consequences of your actions without having to follow every action all the way to the end.

Take chess. You could evaluate a move by playing out the rest of the game. But that’s expensive, and there are many possible continuations. A value function says, approximately, “This position looks promising.” It compresses what you’ve learned from previous games into a judgment you can use immediately.

And it helps with credit assignment. Suppose you do a long sequence of actions and eventually succeed or fail. Which actions were responsible? If you have a good value function, you can notice that after a particular action, your prospects became much better or much worse. That gives you a more local learning signal, even when the actual reward is far away.

But the qualification is that the value function itself has to be learned. You haven’t made the difficulty disappear. If it’s wrong, you can optimize for things that look good to it and don’t actually lead to success. And its judgment depends on what you’re capable of doing afterward. A position might be winning for a very strong player and losing for a weak one.

So I would think of it as a way of reusing experience to make learning and search more efficient. You spend computation discovering what happens, and then you learn to anticipate some of those results.

r001.rationale: It says a value function can estimate the consequences of actions before the agent follows them to the end, providing a more local learning signal while the actual reward is still far away.

r002.rationale: It explains that when prospects become worse after a particular action, that change provides a local learning signal about the action that led there—equivalent to negative feedback on pursuing an unpromising direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main usefulness is that it saves you computation. Suppose you’re playing chess, and you want to know whether a move is good. One way to find out is to play the game to the end. But that’s expensive, especially if you want to consider many different moves. A value function gives you an estimate of how good the resulting position is without having to play everything out.

And that becomes very useful when there’s a long distance between an action and its consequences. You might make a decision now, and only much later discover whether it helped. If you’ve learned a good value function, you can use that estimate to guide your decisions along the way.

Of course, the difficulty is learning a good one. You can have a position that looks promising but actually contains a subtle mistake. The value function needs enough understanding to distinguish those cases. Calling something a value function doesn’t make that understanding easy to acquire.

So you can do reinforcement learning without one. You can sample complete trajectories and learn from the outcomes. But a good value function lets you use your experience more efficiently. You don’t have to rediscover what happens at the end every time you encounter a similar situation.

r001.rationale: It says a value function estimates how good a resulting position is without playing the game to the end, providing guidance before the task is complete.

r002.rationale: It mentions distinguishing promising positions from subtle mistakes, but does not explain that identifying an unpromising reasoning direction gives a negative learning signal for the earlier decision to pursue it.

Of course, the estimate can be wrong, so the interesting question is how reliably you can learn it and how much you should trust it.

luna-5.6.text: A value function is useful because it gives you a compact estimate of how good a state—or a state-action pair—is in terms of future outcomes. That makes learning much more efficient: you can assign credit to earlier decisions, bootstrap from partial experience, and improve the policy without waiting until the very end of an episode. But it’s also a lossy summary of the future. If your model can predict the future in much richer detail, then you may not need to rely on a single scalar value; you can use that broader prediction directly to choose actions. So I see the value function as extremely useful, but not necessarily the final or most general representation of what an intelligent agent needs to know.
